transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood Product), Lena Ortiz (Quantive CTO), Samir Gupta (Quantive ML Eng), Ella Park (Quantive Security)
Shared: migration-playbook.pdf (Redwood), parity-matrix-template.csv (Redwood), quantive-sample-prompts.csv (customer link)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me are Diego, our solutions engineer, and Priya, who owns the product migration playbook. How's the morning over there?
00:07 Lena: Morning, yeah good thanks. We're excited. We've been evaluating options — mostly OpenAI and Anthropic so far — and want to see what Redwood would look like as the replacement runtime and API.
00:15 Maya: Great. Today we'll do a short product walkthrough focused on parity mapping — how calls and behaviors translate from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood's API, plus an ask for sample prompts and perf targets so we can scope a POC.
00:25 Diego: I'll kick off with a quick demo of the Redwood Console and then show code snippets for a one-to-one API swap. Note: some parts of the demo may look slightly different because the console screenshot was from a staging cluster.

02:08 Diego: (screen share) Console home, per-route latency and cost. You'll see that we've got token-level breakdowns — generation tokens vs prompt tokens — and per-route SLOs. For your batch jobs, we recommend pinning to a Dedicated pool for predictable throughput.
02:37 Samir: Quick question — what does "pinning" mean exactly? We currently have a mix of synchronous requests to OpenAI and a couple async batch jobs.
02:43 Diego: Pinning here means reserving capacity (GPU pools) for a model version. If you choose Dedicated, you get reserved instances and autoscaling controls. Hosted will still run on shared capacity but with capacity tiers and fallback policies.
03:02 Ella: From security side, we need to know about KMS/HSM support and audit logs. We have to show SOC 2 and encryption at rest for the board.
03:10 Priya: We support customer-managed keys via KMS integrations and provide audit logs exportable to your SIEM. We can share the security pack after this call.

04:20 Diego: Now, parity. The typical mapping is: OpenAI "messages" -> Redwood chat endpoint; Anthropic "prompt" -> Redwood text endpoint; Together models -> similar text/gen calls but model names differ. For streaming, Redwood supports chunked SSE and WebSocket streaming.
04:47 Samir: Are there differences in stop token behavior or partial token emission? We've seen slight output shifts when switching vendors.
04:55 Diego: Yes, stop behavior can differ. We include a parity-matrix that documents nuances: default temperature handling, logprobs availability, stop sequence precedence. We'll pre-populate with common mappings and tune on your prompts.

06:05 Maya: I'd like to show a concrete code mapping — two lines from OpenAI to Redwood.
06:12 Diego: Sure — OpenAI: openai.ChatCompletion.create({model: 'gpt-4', messages: [...]}) -> Redwood: redwood.chat.generate({model: 'rw-gpt-4x', input: messages, stream: true}) — note param names: input vs messages, and our model catalog uses prefixed model names.
06:34 Samir: And authentication? We currently use API keys with scoped roles.
06:38 Maya: Same model: API keys and short-lived tokens supported, plus per-key usage limits. For SSO and org-level RBAC we support SAML SSO and fine-grained roles via the Console.

08:10 Diego: Performance: you asked about latency headroom. For 2k-context models we typically see median latency of 80-150 ms per token on dedicated NVL48-class instances with our optimized kernels; on hosted it depends on queue and batch. We’ll run benchmark runs with your prompts to validate.
08:41 Lena: That number is good. Our current SLAs require 200ms 95th for interactive features.
08:48 Diego: We can configure routing by latency SLO — requests marked high-priority go to low-latency pools and bypass batching. Lower priority can be batched for cost savings.

10:05 Maya: Cost parity: the economics change with quantization and batching. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per-model and auto-batching settings.
10:20 Samir: Can we keep logprobs and n-best lists? We rely on that for a reranker.
10:25 Diego: Logprobs are available on certain model builds and there's a tradeoff with throughput. We'll flag that in the parity sheet per-model.

12:00 Ella: On data residency: we need data not to leave eu-west-1 for PHI-related tokens. Does Redwood host region pinning?
12:07 Priya: Yes, region pinning is supported in Private and Dedicated setups. Hosted also supports region-level routing for enterprise customers with contractual residency.

13:45 Diego: Switching to a short live demo of an API call. I'll paste a sample mapping we use in the playbook.
13:52 Diego: (typing) Request: POST /v1/chat/generate { input: [{ role: 'user', content: 'summarize patient note...' }], model: 'rw-clinical-7bq', temperature: 0.0 }
14:12 Speaker 1: Uh-huh, so you'd swap model names and input param names, but do you need to rewrite prompts?
14:18 Diego: Usually no rewrite initially; we recommend a small prompt tuning pass because different tokenizers and model pretraining can shift outputs slightly. We'll run a calibration step.

16:00 Samir: About embeddings — we use embeddings for semantic search. Any migration gotchas?
16:06 Diego: Embedding vector lengths may differ across model families. For a mutex-free migration, you can compute new vectors and rebuild indexes, or run dual-lookup for a transitional period. We can provide an incremental reindex runbook.
16:30 Maya: Pro tip: for large corpora, use Redwood Optimize to recommend a batching + cache policy so you amortize token cost.

18:00 Lena: On governance: we need audit trails of who requested what and the prompt that generated the answer. How granular are logs?
18:08 Priya: We store request metadata, prompt hash, model version, and optionally the full prompt content if you enable retention. Logs can be streamed to your S3 or SIEM and are immutable.

20:10 Diego: Now the tricky part — streaming and partial outputs. If your client relies on SSE behavior from OpenAI, Redwood's SSE semantics are similar but the chunking cadence can be different due to batching. We have a fallback: per-request micro-batching disabled for low-latency routes.
20:42 Samir: In practice, that impacts perceived latency. If we have aggressive batching, the first token could be delayed.
20:49 Diego: Correct. That's why we expose batch windows and per-route overrides.

23:00 Maya: Question for Quantive — what's the pilot scope you prefer? Full chat features or embeddings first?
23:08 Lena: Probably embeddings for search + a chat assistant in our clinician dashboard. We want to prove parity on accuracy and latency for the clinician flows.
23:18 Maya: Great. We'll scope the POC around those two verticals.

25:10 Diego: Let's walk through a sample parity matrix item. Row: OpenAI messages -> Redwood chat.generate. Fields: param mapping, streaming support, stop semantics, logprobs availability, tokenization differences, perf estimate. (shows parity-matrix.csv)
25:38 Speaker 1: Could you include an example of a failing parity case?
25:42 Diego: Sure — case: proprietary Together sampling seeds lead to slightly different deterministic outputs. For deterministic production we recommend version locking + post-process normalization on your side.

28:00 Ella: Legal will ask about data deletion and retention timelines. Will Redwood expose APIs to delete customer data?
28:07 Priya: Yes, we provide data deletion APIs and can apply retention policies per-organization. For Dedicated/Private, you can also set local retention policies.

30:15 Maya: Let's cover the Dedicated vs Hosted decision quickly. Dedicated: predictable performance, VPC options, KMS integration, higher fixed price. Hosted: lower start cost, shared pool, faster to launch. Private: full control, on-prem or VPC, for regulated PHI workloads.
30:40 Lena: Sounds like Dedicated is likely for us given latency and PHI needs. We'll want a pricing model we can trial.

33:00 Diego: On deployment rollouts: we support canary routes, model pinning, and automatic fallback to a safe model if an inference failure occurs. You can do A/B by route or by user cohort.
33:28 Samir: Any support for model quantization artifact checks — like a quantization validation report?
33:34 Diego: Yes, Redwood Optimize produces a profile: throughput, perf delta, and logits drift metrics. We'll include that in the POC.

36:00 Maya: Time for an example logprobs/reranker flow: we'll keep logprobs on for the reranker calls but for bulk generation we'll disable to save cost. Diego, show the sample mapping.
36:15 Diego: (typing code) Redwood call: redwood.text.generate({ model: 'rw-gen-13bq', input: prompt, return_logprobs: true, n: 5 }) — we also have a rerank endpoint that accepts candidates and returns a score for faster batch reranking.
36:40 Samir: That rerank endpoint — is it compatible with our current ES-based pipeline?
36:45 Diego: You can call the rerank endpoint and then push top-k IDs to your existing ES index. We support JSON-L payloads so integration is straightforward.

39:15 Lena: Do you have case studies for health customers?
39:20 Maya: Yes, we'll send a short one-page with latency/cost outcomes. Can't disclose names due to NDA but will include architecture patterns.

42:00 Ella: Security drill — if a key is compromised, how fast can we revoke and rollout?
42:06 Priya: Keys are revocable immediately; we issue new keys and you can rotate via SSO/JIT tokens. There's an API for key rotation and a console flow for emergency rotate.

44:40 Maya: Let's capture risk items: a) tokenizer differences leading to edge-case output changes, b) embedding vector dimensionality mismatch c) reranker logprob availability for certain quantized builds. We'll add mitigation steps for each.
44:58 Samir: For tokenizer issues, can you run a tokenization diff?
45:03 Diego: Yes, we can run a tokenization diff on your sample prompts and flag mismatches.

46:20 Maya: Recap and next steps: Diego will prepare the parity matrix and sample SDK snippets by Friday; Priya will attach pricing + deployment options; Quantive will share 500 prompts and target SLAs. We'll schedule the POC planning session next week.

47:10 Lena: Quick operational question — monitoring retention: how long do you keep per-token traces by default?
47:15 Priya: Default is 30 days for hosted; configurable to 90/365 for enterprise plans. For Dedicated we can also enable local retention limits.

49:00 Samir: If we find a regression in model outputs post-migration, what's the rollback plan?
49:06 Diego: You can pin your route to the previous provider (we have a policy engine to route to upstreams) or pin to an earlier model version. We'll recommend a canary rollout and an eval harness to automatically compare outputs.

52:10 Maya: Any final questions?
52:15 Ella: Please include the CISO pack in the follow-up. Also, we might request an encryption architecture diagram.
52:23 Maya: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the parity CSV and POC calendar invite.
52:30 Lena: Thanks all.
52:33 End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-generated, occasional mis-hears ("V P C" instead of "VPC", "K V cache" for "KV cache"). Some speaker attribution is approximate.
